title: How Generative AI Models Work

header.html: Describe how generative AI models work
the official AI-901 study guide, skills measured as of April 15, 2026

toc.title: What generative models can and cannot do

html:
1What generative AI is

Generative AI creates new content (text, code, images, audio) in response to a prompt. The most common kind for text is the large language model (LLM). A smaller, more compact relative is the small language model (SLM).

Term Meaning
Model A trained program that turns an input into an output
Prompt The input you give the model (instructions, question, examples, data)
Completion / response The output the model generates
LLM A large model trained on a very large amount of text, good at general language tasks
SLM A smaller, cheaper, faster model; less general, often enough for focused tasks
Foundation model A broad model trained once and used for many tasks Beyond the study guide

2Tokens

Models do not read words. They read tokens.

  • A token can be a whole word, part of a word (sub-word), punctuation or a space.
  • Every token in the model's vocabulary has a unique integer identifier; text is turned into a sequence of numbers before the model sees it.
  • Cost, speed and limits are counted in tokens: input tokens plus output tokens.
  • Longer words and other languages often use more tokens.

Exam tip

. "The model breaks text into tokens" and "each token has a numeric id". Billing and context limits use tokens, not words or characters.

3The transformer and attention

Modern language models use the transformer architecture.

  • A transformer has two blocks in its original form: an encoder (builds a representation of the input) and a decoder (generates the output). Many text generators use the decoder part.
  • The key idea is attention: for each token, the model looks at the tokens around it and decides how much each one matters, so the meaning of a word depends on its context ("bank" of a river or a bank for money).
  • Models are trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token. To generate text, the model predicts one token, adds it to the input and predicts again, until it stops.

4Embeddings

An embedding is a list (vector) of numbers that represents the meaning of a token or of a whole text.

  • Texts with similar meaning have embeddings that are close together.
  • Closeness is measured with cosine similarity, which compares the angle between two vectors.
  • Uses: semantic search (find documents by meaning, not exact words), recommendation, grouping, and giving a model relevant documents to answer from.
Exam tip

. "Find text with similar meaning" → embeddings and similarity. Plain keyword matching only finds the same words.

Exam tip

. The model has no memory between calls: the application must send the earlier messages again.

5The context window

Every model has a context window: the maximum number of tokens it can handle at once, counting the prompt plus the response.

  • If the prompt is too long, or the requested output would pass the limit, the answer is cut off or the call fails.
  • A model has no memory between calls. For a conversation, the application sends the earlier messages again with each new question.
  • Large windows cost more tokens, so keep prompts focused.

6What generative models can and cannot do

Strength Limit
Writes fluent text, summarizes, translates, answers questions, writes code May produce confident wrong answers (hallucinations)
Follows instructions given in the prompt Knowledge comes from training data and may be out of date
Works across many topics without retraining Cannot check facts by itself unless it is given tools or data
Can be grounded with your own data to answer from it Outputs can vary from one call to the next

Grounding means giving the model trusted data (documents, search results) in the prompt so it answers from them. Beyond the study guide for the full pattern, but the idea is likely to appear.

7Exam Q&A

7.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1Fabrikam Outdoors asks why its AI bill grows when users paste long documents. What is the unit that drives the cost?

  • AWords
  • BCharacters
  • CPages
  • DTokens
Show the answer

Answer: D. Models read and generate tokens, and usage and limits are counted in tokens.

S2Which idea lets a model decide how much each nearby word matters for the meaning of a word?

  • AAttention
  • BCompression
  • CEncryption
  • DSampling
Show the answer

Answer: A. The attention layer examines each token and how it is influenced by the tokens around it.

S3A team wants to find support articles with a similar meaning to a customer's question, even when the words differ. What should it use?

  • AA keyword filter on exact words
  • BEmbeddings and similarity
  • CA larger font in the search box
  • DA spell checker for the articles
Show the answer

Answer: B. Embeddings turn meaning into vectors, and similar vectors point to similar meaning.

S4A chat application must keep the conversation. The model itself has no memory. What does the application do?

  • ANothing; the model remembers every user across all calls
  • BIt retrains the model after each question that a user asks
  • CIt sends the earlier messages again with each new request
  • DIt deletes the system message from every earlier request
Show the answer

Answer: C. Each call is separate, so the app includes the earlier messages (within the context window).

S5What does the context window limit?

  • AThe number of users who can sign in at the same time
  • BThe number of Azure regions where the model runs
  • CThe number of tokens in the prompt plus the response
  • DThe number of images stored in the project
Show the answer

Answer: C. The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can handle at once.

S6A model states a wrong fact in a confident tone. What is this called?

  • ATokenization of the text
  • BA hallucination
  • CEmbedding of the answer
  • DAttention to nearby tokens
Show the answer

Answer: B. A hallucination is a made-up or wrong answer that sounds confident.

7.2 Recall questions

R1What is a token?

Show the answer

A piece of text (word, sub-word or punctuation) that the model reads, with a numeric identifier.

R2What does a language model learn to do during training?

Show the answer

Predict the next token.

R3What is an embedding?

Show the answer

A vector of numbers that represents the meaning of text.

R4What is the context window?

Show the answer

The maximum number of tokens for the prompt plus the response.

R5What is an SLM?

Show the answer

A small language model: more compact, cheaper and faster, less general than an LLM.

R6What does grounding mean?

Show the answer

Giving the model trusted data in the prompt so it answers from that data.

8Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Generative AI creates new content from a prompt; LLMs for text, SLMs are smaller
Tokens words, sub-words, punctuation; numeric ids; cost and limits count tokens
Transformer encoder and decoder; attention weighs nearby tokens; trained to predict the next token
Embeddings vectors of meaning; cosine similarity; semantic search
Context window token limit for prompt plus response; no memory between calls
Limits hallucinations, outdated knowledge; ground with trusted data
